Gerald Ford. The thirty-eighth President of the United States, assuming office in 1974 after Richard Nixon's resignation during the Watergate scandal. Though he served less than two years as president, his decision to pardon Nixon shaped the nation's reckoning with the crisis and defined his presidency.

Gerald Ford was the only U.S. president never elected to either the presidency or vice presidency. He was appointed Vice President after Spiro Agnew's resignation in 1973 and became president when Nixon resigned in 1974. His rise to power was extraordinarily rapid, becoming Vice President in December 1973 and President in August 1974, a span of just eight months. He immediately issued an unconditional pardon of Nixon in September 1974, granting him full forgiveness for crimes related to Watergate.

Ford defended the pardon as necessary for national healing, but it appeared to many as a backroom deal. The pardon proved deeply unpopular, with public approval ratings dropping sharply, and it likely cost him the 1976 presidential election against Jimmy Carter. A career congressman from Michigan for twenty-five years and House Minority Leader before his elevation to the presidency, Ford was known for integrity and bipartisan cooperation in Congress, but had little executive experience before assuming the presidency during a national crisis. He faced foreign policy crises including the fall of Saigon in 1975, the end of American involvement in Vietnam, and the Mayaguez incident with Cambodia. He authorized the military response to the Mayaguez seizure, an action seen as restoring American credibility after Vietnam. Ford lived longer than any other U.S. president and was widely respected for his character, though his pardon of Nixon remained controversial until his death in 2006.
